---
title: "Create Your First Feature"
sidebarTitle: "First Feature"
---

Build is the fastest path from a product requirement to a reviewed code change. Use it when you know what the application should do and want Revolte to generate the implementation, tests, and pull request around that intent.

This guide walks through two layers of setup:

- Completing the first workspace and application setup
- Submitting a focused build request that produces a pull request

## New to Revolte?

Build is one part of a larger delivery loop. If you land here first, use this quick model:

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="Build">
    Describe a requirement. Revolte generates code, tests, documentation, and a pull request.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Deploy">
    Merge approved work. Revolte releases it through preview, QA, staging, or production.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Observe">
    Check logs, metrics, and activity to confirm the release is healthy.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Control">
    Manage users, roles, services, secrets, storage, and scheduled jobs.
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

> ✅ **Need the product overview first?**  
> Read [Introduction to Revolte](/docs) to understand the full platform in 2 to 5 minutes.

> ⚠️ **Prerequisite**  
> You need a Git repository that Revolte can read and write to, plus the required permissions from your Git provider.

## Before you start

Make sure you have:

- A repository you want Revolte to manage
- Access to the branch where Revolte should open pull requests
- Any required repository permissions from your Git provider
- A clear idea of the application or system you want to set up

## Visual setup walkthrough

If you are new to Revolte, complete the guided setup before submitting your first build request. The screenshots below follow the onboarding flow in order, from `quick-start-1` through `quick-start-8`.

This setup gives Revolte the context it needs to generate code safely: workspace details, repository access, project mapping, application configuration, and deployment pipeline settings.

<Steps>
  <Step title="Sign up">
    Create your Revolte account to begin the onboarding flow. This gives you access to the workspace, project, and application setup that follows.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Complete workspace details">
    Confirm your organization details and role so Revolte can tailor the workspace context.

    ![Workspace details modal for entering organization name, role, and referral source](/images/quickstart/quick-start-1.png)
  </Step>

  <Step title="Select a cloud target">
    Choose where Revolte should run and manage the application infrastructure.

    ![Cloud target selection with Revolte Cloud selected](/images/quickstart/quick-start-2.png)
  </Step>

  <Step title="Connect source control">
    Connect the Git provider that contains the repository Revolte should use for generated pull requests.

    ![Source control integration options with GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and custom token fields](/images/quickstart/quick-start-3.png)
  </Step>

  <Step title="Connect project management">
    Optionally connect a product management tool so issues or requirements can be linked to build workflows.

    ![Project management integration step with Jira selected](/images/quickstart/quick-start-4.png)
  </Step>

  <Step title="Create the project">
    Create or select the project that will group related applications under the same product context.

    ![Project creation form with project name and Jira project mapping](/images/quickstart/quick-start-5.png)
  </Step>

  <Step title="Create the application">
    Name the application and select the repository Revolte should manage.

    ![Application creation form with application name and repository selection](/images/quickstart/quick-start-6.png)
  </Step>

  <Step title="Configure the pipeline">
    Review the generated configuration, framework selection, branch mapping, and workflow toggles.

    ![Pipeline configuration screen showing framework, branch mapping, workflow toggles, and generated YAML](/images/quickstart/quick-start-7.png)
  </Step>

  <Step title="Launch the application">
    Confirm the launch checklist and start the first deployment workflow.

    ![Launch confirmation checklist over generated Revolte configuration](/images/quickstart/quick-start-8.png)
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Submit your first build

After the application is connected and the pipeline is configured, use Build to generate your first implementation.

<Steps>
  <Step title="Open the application">
    From your workspace, select the project and application you want to change. Revolte uses this context to understand repository structure, framework conventions, branch mapping, and deployment targets.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Describe the requirement">
    Write the requirement in plain language. Focus on behavior, inputs, outputs, validation, and expected edge cases.

    ```txt
    Add a REST endpoint that returns a user's recent activity with pagination, authentication, and tests.
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step title="Let Revolte generate the change">
    Revolte analyzes the repository, plans the implementation, modifies code, creates tests, and prepares supporting documentation where needed.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Review the pull request">
    Inspect the generated pull request like any teammate's change. Check the diff, tests, configuration updates, and implementation summary before approving.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Merge when ready">
    After approval, merge the pull request. Deploy can then release the application according to your configured pipeline and environment rules.
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Write a strong requirement

A good Build request tells Revolte what should be true after the change lands.

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Good">
    ```txt
    Add JWT authentication to the user profile API. Require a valid bearer token, return 401 for missing or invalid tokens, and add tests for success, missing token, and expired token cases.
    ```
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="Too vague">
    ```txt
    Add auth.
    ```
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

Include:

- The user-facing or API behavior
- Inputs and expected outputs
- Authentication or permission rules
- Existing patterns Revolte should follow
- Error states that should be handled
- Test expectations for critical paths

## What you should receive

A successful build should produce:

- Source changes scoped to the requirement
- Unit or integration tests for the new behavior
- Documentation updates when the change affects usage or operation
- A pull request with implementation context and validation evidence
